title: The serpent who teaches the seat
hook: the serpent who holds up Vishnu comes down as a teacher, and starts with how to sit
carry: posture and breath are rungs toward a still mind
tomorrow: who taught yoga first, and who overheard?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: a student asked too much, and the teacher drew breath as a king sending officers out to the villages.

Out on the cosmic ocean, Vishnu rests on a great serpent with a thousand heads. Its name is Shesha, also called Ananta, the endless. It holds him steady, coiled and at ease, through the long night between worlds. Tradition tells that this serpent once came down to teach. A woman named Gonika stood praying with her palms cupped, and a tiny snake dropped into them. He grew up to be Patanjali, the teacher of the Yoga Sutras; tradition hears his name as fallen, pata, into folded palms, anjali. Today: what he teaches about sitting, breathing, and what both are for.
screen: `VISHNU'S SERPENT SEAT.` → `A SNAKE IN CUPPED HANDS.` → `PATANJALI, TEACHER OF THE SEAT.`

segments.voice: That's a legend from later tradition; the Sutras never tell his life. But notice what it makes of him: the serpent who is God's own couch becomes the teacher of the seat. Patanjali opens with yoga's aim, in paraphrase: yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind, and then the seer rests in its own nature. That's the big teaching. In Hindu yoga the goal isn't a body. It's a mind quiet enough for the self, the seer, to be seen. To get there he lays out eight limbs, ashtanga. First, how you treat others and yourself. Then posture, then breath, and on up to meditation and absorption. Posture and breath are rungs three and four. Now the seat. Patanjali asks for one that is steady and easy, sthira and sukha. It comes, he says, as effort loosens and the mind rests on the endless, ananta. Some teachers hear the serpent's own name in that word: sit the way Ananta holds Vishnu, firm and at ease. That's a reading, not the text. Only after the seat comes pranayama, which he defines as a pause in the flow of breathing in and breathing out. Not a push. Its fruit: the mind becomes fit for concentration. Some yoga classes open with a chant bowing to Patanjali as that white, thousand-headed serpent. They're borrowing a ladder whose top is the self. So when a class feels like a workout, remember: the stretch is a low rung, and the climb is toward a quiet mind. If you have heart or lung trouble, or get dizzy, keep breath practice gentle and ask a doctor first.
screen: `YOGA: A STILL MIND` · `POSTURE AND BREATH: RUNGS 3 AND 4` · `A STEADY, EASY SEAT; THEN A PAUSE` · `THE STRETCH IS A LOW RUNG`

segments.voice: Sit the way the serpent holds Vishnu: steady first, then easy, shoulders down, jaw loose, effort loosening a little with each breath out. Only then turn to the breath, and don't steer it; if a natural little pause comes after a breath out, notice it without stretching it, and if anything strains, go back to the seat. If you pray, you can let the stillness be your prayer.
The breath again. In Patanjali, a steady, easy seat comes first, and pranayama is a pause in the flow of breath, both rungs toward a still mind. Today's word.
Your line: posture and breath are rungs toward a still mind. Patanjali's ladder ends in the self. See you tomorrow.

Patanjali.meaning: the teacher behind the Yoga Sutras

Shesha.meaning: the thousand-headed serpent Vishnu rests on, also called Ananta

ashtanga.meaning: eight limbs: Patanjali's ladder from conduct to absorption

sthira.meaning: steady: the first mark of a good seat

sukha.meaning: easy: the second mark of a good seat

pranayama.meaning: in Patanjali, a pause in the flow of breathing in and out

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 1.2–1.3 (yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind; then the seer rests in its own nature)
Yoga Sutras 2.46–2.49 (a steady, easy seat; effort loosened, the mind resting on the endless; then pranayama, the pause in the flow of in-breath and out-breath)
Yoga Sutras 2.52–2.53 (the covering of the light thins; the mind fit for concentration)

Traditional legend of Patanjali as an incarnation of Shesha (Ananta), falling into Gonika's cupped hands (the name read as pata + anjali); the invocation to Patanjali as the thousand-headed white serpent
sources.work: later Hindu tradition (legend; not in the Sutras)
